query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing manganese content in steels with a fixed chromium content reduces the rate of chromium dissolution in corrosive molten fluoride salt environments by promoting the formation of stable manganese fluoride compounds, which in turn helps preserve a protective chromium-based passive film.
generation.material_initial_state: Steel alloys containing approximately 18 wt.% chromium and varying manganese contents (e.g., ~2 wt.% in baseline steels versus ~6 wt.% in modified steels)
generation.intervention: Expose the steels to a controlled molten fluoride salt environment at high temperature, replicating the conditions typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications
generation.conditions: Molten salt with low levels of impurities (e.g., controlled moisture content) at temperatures representative of reactor or processing conditions, for a duration sufficient to observe measurable corrosion and film evolution
generation.structural_mediator: A protective surface film comprising chromium oxides (or related compounds) whose integrity is maintained by inhibited chromium dissolution due to preferential manganese reaction in the salt
generation.mechanism: Because manganese forms MnF2 at a lower Gibbs free energy than chromium forms CrF2, a higher Mn content results in selective Mn dissolution. This process reduces the exposure of chromium to the aggressive environment, thereby supporting the persistence of a self-healing, chromium-based passive layer that retards further corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline low-Mn steel, the higher-Mn steel is expected to show lower chromium loss (as measured by surface analysis and salt composition), reduced overall mass loss, and improved stability of the passive film during exposure to molten fluoride salts
generation.baseline: Steels with around 2 wt.% Mn and 18 wt.% Cr that experience higher levels of Cr dissolution and less robust passive film formation in the same corrosive environment
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate in high-temperature molten fluoride salt environments typical of nuclear reactors and certain chemical-processing systems. The hypothesis may not hold in aqueous or typical atmospheric oxidation conditions where different corrosion mechanisms dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the corrosion rate reduction and the detailed characteristics of the protective film depend on factors such as precise alloy composition, salt impurities, exposure time, and temperature; quantitative values are currently uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples with the same Cr content (~18 wt.%) but differing Mn contents (one with ~2 wt.% Mn as the baseline and one with ~6 wt.% Mn). Expose both sample sets to identical molten fluoride salt environments at controlled high temperature for a fixed period. Post-exposure, analyze the samples for mass loss, element leaching into the salt, and integrity of the surface passive film using techniques such as SEM-EDS, ICP-MS, and XRD.
measurements: Mass loss of samples over time
Concentrations of Cr and Mn in the molten salt (via ICP-MS)
Surface film composition and morphology (via SEM-EDS and XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-Mn steel does not show a statistically significant reduction in chromium loss, improved film integrity (e.g., thickness, continuity), or lower overall mass loss compared to the baseline low-Mn steel, then the hypothesis that enhanced manganese content protects against Cr dissolution by favoring MnF2 formation and preserving a Cr-based passive film will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion behavior

Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy [2] . Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion [2] .
